```{r read-data}
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# Read the cleaned data and shorten long category labels
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
data <- read_excel("commuter-survey-cleaned.xlsx", sheet = "Cleaned data")

data <- data %>%
  mutate(
    faculty = recode(faculty,
      "Management Studies and Commerce" = "Management & Commerce"),
    main_mode = recode(main_mode,
      "Private vehicle (own, or dropped by someone)" = "Private vehicle",
      "Three-wheeler / PickMe / Uber"                = "Three-wheeler / taxi"),
    access_mode = recode(access_mode,
      "None / Direct access (I step straight onto my main transport from home)" = "Direct access"),
    egress_mode = recode(egress_mode,
      "None / Direct drop-off (My main transport drops me right at the university gate)" = "Direct drop-off"),
    seat = recode(seat,
      "Usually get a seat"              = "Get a seat",
      "Usually stand"                   = "Stand",
      "Not applicable (walk / bicycle)" = "Not applicable"),
    late_arrivals = recode(late_arrivals,
      "0 days per week (Never)" = "Never",
      "1 day per week"          = "1 day/week",
      "2–3 days per week"       = "2–3 days/week",
      "4+ days per week"        = "4+ days/week"),
    travel_budget = recode(travel_budget,
      "Nothing (0% — Free / Walk)" = "Nothing (0%)",
      "10% to 25%"                 = "10%–25%",
      "26% to 50%"                 = "26%–50%"),
    crowding = sub(" \\(.*", "", crowding)    # keep "Very crowded", drop the description
  )
```

```{r set-order}
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# Order of categories
#   Ordinal variables: natural order (low to high)
#   Nominal variables: most frequent first ("Other ..." last)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
ordinal_levels <- list(
  days_per_week     = c("3–4 days", "5 days or more"),
  study_year        = c("1st year", "2nd year", "3rd year", "4th year", "5th year or above"),
  distance          = c("Less than 5 km", "5–14 km", "15–29 km", "30–49 km", "50 km or more"),
  vehicle_changes   = c("No change", "1 change", "2 changes", "3 or more changes"),
  late_arrivals     = c("Never", "1 day/week", "2–3 days/week", "4+ days/week"),
  trip_time         = c("Under 30 min", "30–59 min", "1 to 1½ hours", "1½ to 2 hours", "Over 2 hours"),
  wait_time         = c("I don't wait", "Under 5 min", "5–15 min", "15–30 min", "Over 30 min"),
  departure_time    = c("Before 6:00 am", "6:00–6:59 am", "7:00–7:59 am", "8:00 am or later"),
  travel_budget     = c("Nothing (0%)", "Less than 10%", "10%–25%", "26%–50%", "More than 50%"),
  feel_unsafe       = c("Never", "Rarely", "Sometimes", "Often"),
  stressed_relaxed  = c("-3 Very stressed", "-2 Quite stressed", "-1 Slightly stressed", "0 Neither",
                        "+1 Slightly relaxed", "+2 Quite relaxed", "+3 Very relaxed"),
  worried_confident = c("-3 Very worried", "-2 Quite worried", "-1 Slightly worried", "0 Neither",
                        "+1 Slightly confident", "+2 Quite confident", "+3 Very confident"),
  hurried_calm      = c("-3 Very hurried", "-2 Quite hurried", "-1 Slightly hurried", "0 Neither",
                        "+1 Slightly calm", "+2 Quite calm", "+3 Very calm"),
  stress_these_days = c("Not at all", "Only a little", "To some extent", "Rather much", "Very much"),
  sleep_quality     = c("Very poor", "Poor", "Average", "Good", "Very good"),
  workload_pressure = c("Very low", "Low", "Moderate", "High", "Very high"),
  crowding          = c("Not crowded", "Slightly crowded", "Moderately crowded",
                        "Very crowded", "Extremely crowded"),
  weather_impact    = c("Not at all", "Slightly", "Moderately", "Very much", "Extremely"),
  stress_level      = c("Low", "Moderate", "High")
)
nominal_vars <- c("faculty", "gender", "residence", "main_mode", "access_mode", "egress_mode", "seat")

for (v in names(ordinal_levels)) {
  data[[v]] <- factor(data[[v]], levels = ordinal_levels[[v]])
}
for (v in nominal_vars) {
  freq <- sort(table(data[[v]]), decreasing = TRUE)
  lv   <- names(freq)
  lv   <- c(lv[!grepl("^Other", lv)], lv[grepl("^Other", lv)])
  data[[v]] <- factor(data[[v]], levels = lv)
}

# Safety check: a label that did not match its list would turn into NA.
# crowding is the only variable allowed to have blanks (non bus/train users).
bad <- sapply(setdiff(c(names(ordinal_levels), nominal_vars), "crowding"),
              function(v) sum(is.na(data[[v]])))
if (any(bad > 0)) stop("Unmatched labels in: ", paste(names(bad)[bad > 0], collapse = ", "))
```

```{r merged-data}
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# Merged categories for the two- and three-variable analysis
# (groups with only 1-3 students give unreliable percentages).
# Section 1.1 uses the original categories in `data`.
# Edit or delete lines here as needed.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
merge_levels <- function(f, old, new) {
  levels(f)[levels(f) %in% old] <- new
  f
}

data_m <- data %>%
  mutate(
    distance          = merge_levels(distance, c("30–49 km", "50 km or more"), "30 km or more"),
    wait_time         = merge_levels(wait_time, c("15–30 min", "Over 30 min"), "15 min or more"),
    late_arrivals     = merge_levels(late_arrivals, c("2–3 days/week", "4+ days/week"), "2+ days/week"),
    workload_pressure = merge_levels(workload_pressure, c("Very low", "Low"), "Low"),
    crowding          = merge_levels(crowding, c("Not crowded", "Slightly crowded"), "Not/slightly crowded"),

    # Broader groups used in the three-variable analysis (Section 1.3)
    trip_time3 = merge_levels(trip_time, c("1 to 1½ hours", "1½ to 2 hours", "Over 2 hours"),
                              "1 hour or more"),
    mode2      = factor(case_when(main_mode %in% c("Bus", "Train")  ~ "Bus / train",
                                  main_mode == "Walk or bicycle"     ~ "Walk / bicycle",
                                  TRUE                               ~ "Private / hired"),
                        levels = c("Bus / train", "Private / hired", "Walk / bicycle")),
    distance2  = factor(ifelse(distance %in% c("Less than 5 km", "5–14 km"),
                               "Under 15 km", "15 km or more"),
                        levels = c("Under 15 km", "15 km or more"))
  )
```

```{r helpers}
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# Helper functions (you normally do not need to edit these)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------

# Common look for every graph
theme_report <- function() {
  theme_classic(base_size = 13, base_family = FONT) +
    theme(axis.text          = element_text(colour = "black", size = 12),
          axis.title         = element_text(colour = "black", size = 13),
          legend.text        = element_text(colour = "black", size = 12),
          legend.title       = element_text(colour = "black", size = 12),
          strip.text         = element_text(colour = "black", size = 12),
          strip.background   = element_rect(fill = "#f0efec", colour = NA),
          panel.grid.major.y = element_line(colour = "#e1e0d9", linewidth = 0.3),
          legend.position    = "right")
}

wrap_text <- function(x, width = 22) paste(strwrap(x, width), collapse = "\n")

# Colours for a variable, based on its type
palette_for <- function(var, n) {
  if (var %in% c("stressed_relaxed", "worried_confident", "hurried_calm") && n == 7) return(diverging7)
  if (var %in% nominal_vars || var == "mode2") return(nominal_cols[seq_len(n)])
  if (n == 1) return(blues[5])
  blues[round(seq(1, length(blues), length.out = n))]
}

# Save a graph to the figures folder (PNG, 300 dpi)
save_fig <- function(p, name, width = 7.5, height = 4.5) {
  ggsave(file.path("figures", paste0(name, ".png")), p, device = ragg::agg_png,
         width = width, height = height, dpi = 300, bg = "white")
  invisible(p)
}

# Collect every table; all are written to tables/analysis-tables.xlsx at the end
table_list  <- list()
table_index <- data.frame(Sheet = character(), Table = character())
add_table <- function(df, description) {
  sheet <- sprintf("T%02d", length(table_list) + 1)
  table_list[[sheet]] <<- df
  table_index[nrow(table_index) + 1, ] <<- c(sheet, description)
}

# ---- One qualitative variable: frequency table + bar or pie chart ----
one_var <- function(var, chart = c("bar", "pie"), df = data) {
  chart <- match.arg(chart)
  x   <- df[[var]][!is.na(df[[var]])]
  tb  <- table(droplevels(x))
  tab <- data.frame(Category   = names(tb),
                    Count      = as.integer(tb),
                    Percentage = round(100 * as.integer(tb) / sum(tb), 2))
  tab$Category <- factor(tab$Category, levels = names(tb))
  cols <- palette_for(var, nrow(tab))

  if (chart == "bar") {
    p <- ggplot(tab, aes(x = Category, y = Count, fill = Category)) +
      geom_col(width = 0.7) +
      geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.1f%%", Percentage)),
                vjust = -0.4, family = FONT, size = 4.2) +
      scale_fill_manual(values = cols, name = wrap_text(lab[[var]]),
                        labels = function(l) sapply(l, wrap_text, width = 25)) +
      scale_x_discrete(name = lab[[var]], labels = label_wrap(ifelse(nrow(tab) >= 6, 9, 14))) +
      scale_y_continuous(name = "Number of students",
                         expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.12))) +
      theme_report()
  } else {
    tab$Label <- sprintf("%.1f%%\n(n = %d)", tab$Percentage, tab$Count)
    p <- ggplot(tab, aes(x = "", y = Count, fill = Category)) +
      geom_col(width = 1, colour = "white", linewidth = 0.8) +
      coord_polar(theta = "y", start = 0) +
      geom_text(aes(label = Label), position = position_stack(vjust = 0.5),
                family = FONT, size = 5, colour = "white") +
      scale_fill_manual(values = cols, name = lab[[var]]) +
      theme_void(base_family = FONT, base_size = 13) +
      theme(legend.text  = element_text(size = 13),
            legend.title = element_text(size = 13))
  }
  save_fig(p, paste0("1.1_", var), width = ifelse(nrow(tab) >= 6, 9.5, 7.5))

  out <- tab[, c("Category", "Count", "Percentage")]
  out$Category <- as.character(out$Category)
  out <- rbind(out, data.frame(Category = "Total", Count = sum(out$Count), Percentage = 100))
  names(out)[1] <- lab[[var]]
  add_table(out, paste0("1.1 Frequency table: ", lab[[var]]))

  list(table = kable(out, align = "lrr"), plot = p)
}

# Build an "n (row %)" two-way table from counts
format_two_way <- function(tb, row_title) {
  pct  <- 100 * prop.table(tb, 1)
  disp <- matrix(sprintf("%d (%.1f%%)", tb, pct), nrow = nrow(tb),
                 dimnames = dimnames(tb))
  out  <- data.frame(Group = rownames(tb), disp, Total = sprintf("%d (100%%)", rowSums(tb)),
                     check.names = FALSE)
  ct   <- colSums(tb)
  out  <- rbind(out, c("Total", sprintf("%d (%.1f%%)", ct, 100 * ct / sum(tb)),
                       sprintf("%d (100%%)", sum(tb))))
  names(out)[1] <- row_title
  out
}

# ---- Two qualitative variables: table with row % + clustered bar chart ----
two_way <- function(row, col, df = data_m) {
  d  <- df[!is.na(df[[row]]) & !is.na(df[[col]]), ]
  tb <- table(droplevels(d[[row]]), droplevels(d[[col]]))
  out <- format_two_way(tb, lab[[row]])
  add_table(out, paste0("1.2 ", lab[[col]], " by ", tolower(lab[[row]]), " (row %)"))

  pd <- as.data.frame(tb)
  names(pd) <- c("row", "col", "n")
  pd$pct <- 100 * pd$n / ave(pd$n, pd$row, FUN = sum)
  nbars  <- nrow(pd)

  p <- ggplot(pd, aes(x = row, y = pct, fill = col)) +
    geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = 0.85), width = 0.8) +
    geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.0f%%", pct)),
              position = position_dodge(width = 0.85), vjust = -0.4,
              family = FONT, size = ifelse(nbars > 16, 3.2, 3.8)) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = palette_for(col, nlevels(pd$col)),
                      name = wrap_text(lab[[col]]),
                      labels = function(l) sapply(l, wrap_text, width = 22)) +
    scale_x_discrete(name = lab[[row]], labels = label_wrap(14)) +
    scale_y_continuous(name = wrap_text(paste0("Percentage within ", tolower(lab[[row]]), " (%)"), 30),
                       limits = c(0, NA), expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.12))) +
    theme_report()
  save_fig(p, paste0("1.2_", row, "_x_", col), width = 9, height = 5)

  list(table = kable(out, align = c("l", rep("r", ncol(out) - 1))), plot = p,
       n = sum(tb))
}

# ---- Three qualitative variables: table + clustered bars in panels ----
three_way <- function(row, panel, col, df = data_m) {
  d  <- df[!is.na(df[[row]]) & !is.na(df[[col]]) & !is.na(df[[panel]]), ]
  d[[row]] <- droplevels(d[[row]]); d[[col]] <- droplevels(d[[col]]); d[[panel]] <- droplevels(d[[panel]])

  parts <- lapply(levels(d[[panel]]), function(pl) {
    s  <- d[d[[panel]] == pl, ]
    tb <- table(s[[row]], s[[col]])
    tb <- tb[rowSums(tb) > 0, , drop = FALSE]
    o  <- format_two_way(tb, lab[[row]])
    cbind(setNames(data.frame(c(pl, rep("", nrow(o) - 1))), lab[[panel]]), o)
  })
  out <- do.call(rbind, parts)
  add_table(out, paste0("1.3 ", lab[[col]], " by ", tolower(lab[[row]]), " and ", tolower(lab[[panel]]), " (row %)"))

  pd <- as.data.frame(table(d[[panel]], d[[row]], d[[col]]))
  names(pd) <- c("panel", "row", "col", "n")
  tot <- ave(pd$n, pd$panel, pd$row, FUN = sum)
  pd  <- pd[tot > 0, ]
  pd$pct <- 100 * pd$n / tot[tot > 0]
  pd$panel <- paste0(lab[[panel]], ": ", pd$panel)
  pd$panel <- factor(pd$panel, levels = unique(pd$panel))

  p <- ggplot(pd, aes(x = row, y = pct, fill = col)) +
    geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = 0.85), width = 0.8) +
    geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.0f%%", pct)),
              position = position_dodge(width = 0.85), vjust = -0.4,
              family = FONT, size = 3.4) +
    facet_wrap(~ panel, scales = "free_x") +   # each panel shows only its own groups
    scale_fill_manual(values = palette_for(col, nlevels(pd$col)), name = wrap_text(lab[[col]])) +
    scale_x_discrete(name = lab[[row]], labels = label_wrap(12)) +
    scale_y_continuous(name = "Percentage within group (%)",
                       limits = c(0, NA), expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.12))) +
    theme_report()
  save_fig(p, paste0("1.3_", col, "_by_", row, "_and_", panel), width = 10, height = 5)

  list(table = kable(out, align = c("l", "l", rep("r", ncol(out) - 2))), plot = p,
       n = nrow(d))
}

# Turn a "-2 Quite stressed" style label into its number (-2)
score_of <- function(x) as.numeric(sub(" .*", "", as.character(x)))
```

# 0. Checking the stress score 

The stress score is built from three questions (C1–C3). Before using it, check
that (a) the three questions measure the same thing (**reliability**, Cronbach's
alpha) and (b) the score agrees with a separate stress question, C4
(**convergent validity**, Spearman correlation).

## 0.1 Reliability: Cronbach's alpha

Cronbach's alpha shows how consistently the three items move together. It runs
from 0 to 1:

| Alpha | Reliability |
|---|---|
| 0.90 or above | Excellent |
| 0.80 – 0.89 | Good |
| 0.70 – 0.79 | Acceptable |
| 0.60 – 0.69 | Questionable |
| Below 0.60 | Poor |

The guide's cut-off is **alpha ≥ 0.70**. "Alpha if item deleted" shows what
alpha would be without each item. If removing an item makes alpha clearly
higher, that item does not fit well with the others.

```{r cronbach}
items <- data.frame(C1 = score_of(data$stressed_relaxed),
                    C2 = score_of(data$worried_confident),
                    C3 = score_of(data$hurried_calm))

cronbach_alpha <- function(x) {
  k <- ncol(x)
  (k / (k - 1)) * (1 - sum(apply(x, 2, var)) / var(rowSums(x)))
}

alpha <- cronbach_alpha(items)

item_stats <- data.frame(
  Item = c("C1 Stressed – relaxed", "C2 Worried – confident", "C3 Hurried – calm"),
  `Item-total correlation` = sapply(names(items), function(i)
    round(cor(items[[i]], rowSums(items[setdiff(names(items), i)])), 3)),
  `Alpha if item deleted` = sapply(names(items), function(i)
    round(cronbach_alpha(items[setdiff(names(items), i)]), 3)),
  check.names = FALSE, row.names = NULL)

add_table(data.frame(Measure = "Cronbach's alpha (C1–C3)", Value = round(alpha, 3)),
          "0.1 Cronbach's alpha")
add_table(item_stats, "0.1 Item statistics")

kable(data.frame(Measure = "Cronbach's alpha (C1–C3)", `Number of items` = 3,
                 Alpha = round(alpha, 3), check.names = FALSE))
kable(item_stats)
```

Cronbach's alpha = **`r round(alpha, 3)`**.

Cronbach's alpha for the three stress items (C1–C3) is 0.845, which indicates good internal consistency and is above the 0.70 cut-off given in the guide. Each item correlates strongly with the total of the other two (item–total correlations from 0.665 to 0.749), and removing any one item would lower alpha (to between 0.749 and 0.829). The three items therefore measure one underlying construct, and it is appropriate to combine them into a single stress score.

## 0.2 Convergent validity: Spearman correlation with C4

C4 ("Do you feel this kind of stress these days?") is coded 1 = Not at all to
5 = Very much. A significant **positive** correlation (p < 0.05) means students
with higher stress scores also report more stress in C4, so the score reflects
real stress.

```{r spearman}
c4 <- as.numeric(data$stress_these_days)   # 1 = Not at all ... 5 = Very much
sp <- cor.test(data$stress_score, c4, method = "spearman", exact = FALSE)

sp_tab <- data.frame(Variables = "Stress score vs C4 (stress these days)",
                     `Spearman's rho` = round(unname(sp$estimate), 3),
                     `p-value` = signif(sp$p.value, 3),
                     n = sum(!is.na(c4)), check.names = FALSE)
add_table(sp_tab, "0.2 Spearman correlation: stress score vs C4")
kable(sp_tab)
```

The stress score has a positive and statistically significant Spearman correlation with C4 (ρ = 0.196, p = 0.024, n = 132). Students with higher commute stress scores also tend to report more stress in general, which supports the convergent validity of the score. The correlation is weak, which is expected, because C1–C3 refer specifically to the commute while C4 asks about stress in daily life as a whole.

# 1. Composition of the sample

## 1.1 One qualitative variable

Each graph is saved in the **figures** folder as a 300 dpi PNG file.

### 1.1.1 Respondent profile

#### Days per week travelling to university

```{r v-days-per-week}
res <- one_var("days_per_week", chart = "bar")
res$table
res$plot
```

Slightly more than half of the students (53.03%, 70 students) travel to the university 3–4 days a week, while 46.97% (62 students) travel 5 days or more. Almost half of the sample therefore commutes on every working day, so commute conditions are a regular part of their week.


#### Faculty

```{r v-faculty}
res <- one_var("faculty", chart = "bar")
res$table
res$plot
```

Half of the respondents (50.00%, 66 students) are from the Faculty of Applied Sciences. Management & Commerce (12.88%) and Engineering (11.36%) are the next largest groups, followed by Computing (8.33%) and Technology (6.82%), while the remaining faculties together account for 10.61%. The sample is therefore dominated by Applied Sciences students, which should be kept in mind when generalising the results to all undergraduates.


#### Year of study

```{r v-study-year}
res <- one_var("study_year", chart = "bar")
res$table
res$plot
```

Third-year students form the majority of the sample (56.82%, 75 students), followed by second-year (21.97%) and fourth-year students (12.12%). First-year students (7.58%) and students in their fifth year or above (1.52%) are few. The results therefore mainly reflect the experience of students in the middle of their degree.


#### Gender

```{r v-gender}
res <- one_var("gender", chart = "pie")
res$table
res$plot
```

The sample is fairly balanced by gender: 53.79% (71) of the respondents are male and 46.21% (61) are female.


#### Residence during semester

```{r v-residence}
res <- one_var("residence", chart = "bar")
res$table
res$plot
```

Most students (78.79%, 104) live at home during the semester (including one student who stays at a relative's home), while 15.15% (20) stay in a boarding place and 6.06% (8) in a university hostel. The commute experience described in this study is therefore mainly that of students travelling from home.


### 1.1.2 Travel characteristics

#### One-way distance to university

```{r v-distance}
res <- one_var("distance", chart = "bar")
res$table
res$plot
```

One-way distances are spread fairly evenly across the first three groups: 27.27% of students live less than 5 km from the university, 29.55% live 5–14 km away and 33.33% live 15–29 km away. Only 9.09% travel 30–49 km and a single student (0.76%) travels 50 km or more. In total, 43.18% of students travel 15 km or more each way.


#### Main transport mode

```{r v-main-mode}
res <- one_var("main_mode", chart = "bar")
res$table
res$plot
```

The bus is by far the most common main mode of transport, used by more than half of the students (55.30%, 73). Private vehicles come second (20.45%), followed by walking or cycling (13.64%), three-wheelers or taxis (6.06%) and the train (4.55%). Public transport (bus and train) therefore carries 59.85% of the sample.


#### Number of vehicle changes

```{r v-vehicle-changes}
res <- one_var("vehicle_changes", chart = "bar")
res$table
res$plot
```

Nearly half of the students (46.97%) reach the university without changing vehicles. However, 26.52% change once, 19.70% change twice and 6.82% change three or more times, so more than half (53.03%) make at least one transfer on the way to the university.


#### Mode from home to main vehicle

```{r v-access-mode}
res <- one_var("access_mode", chart = "bar")
res$table
res$plot
```

To reach their main vehicle, 44.70% of the students walk and 33.33% have direct access (they board their main transport at home). Smaller groups are dropped off by someone (10.61%), use a three-wheeler (7.58%) or take a bus (3.79%). Walking is therefore the main way of reaching the main vehicle.


#### Mode from main vehicle to university gate

```{r v-egress-mode}
res <- one_var("egress_mode", chart = "bar")
res$table
res$plot
```

From the main vehicle to the university gate, almost half of the students walk (48.48%) and one-third are dropped directly at the gate (33.33%). A further 16.67% take a three-wheeler for the last stretch, while only 1.52% use a bus.


#### Seat availability

```{r v-seat}
res <- one_var("seat", chart = "bar")
res$table
res$plot
```

Among all respondents, 46.21% usually get a seat and 25.00% usually stand, while 28.79% answered 'not applicable' (mainly those who walk, cycle or use a private vehicle). Among the 94 students for whom the question applies, about one in three (35.1%) usually has to stand.


#### Late arrivals (15+ minutes)

```{r v-late-arrivals}
res <- one_var("late_arrivals", chart = "bar")
res$table
res$plot
```

Just over one-third of the students (35.61%) never arrive 15 or more minutes late, while 34.09% are late one day a week and 28.03% two to three days a week. Very few (2.27%) are late four or more days a week. Overall, almost two-thirds of the students (64.39%) arrive late at least once a week.


#### One-way trip time

```{r v-trip-time}
res <- one_var("trip_time", chart = "bar")
res$table
res$plot
```

One-third of the students (33.33%) reach the university in under 30 minutes and 26.52% take 30–59 minutes. However, 40.15% spend an hour or more on a one-way trip: 18.18% take 1 to 1½ hours, 17.42% take 1½ to 2 hours and 4.55% take over 2 hours.


#### Waiting time for vehicle

```{r v-wait-time}
res <- one_var("wait_time", chart = "bar")
res$table
res$plot
```

The most common waiting time for a vehicle is 5–15 minutes (36.36%). About one-third of the students (32.58%) do not wait at all and 18.94% wait less than 5 minutes. A smaller group waits 15–30 minutes (11.36%) and one student (0.76%) waits over 30 minutes.


#### Departure time

```{r v-departure-time}
res <- one_var("departure_time", chart = "bar")
res$table
res$plot
```

Most students leave for the university between 6:00 and 7:59 am (38.64% between 6:00 and 6:59 am and 39.39% between 7:00 and 7:59 am). About one in nine (11.36%) leave before 6:00 am, while 10.61% leave at 8:00 am or later.


#### Share of daily budget spent on travel

```{r v-travel-budget}
res <- one_var("travel_budget", chart = "bar")
res$table
res$plot
```

The share of the daily budget spent on travel varies widely. The largest group spends 10%–25% (27.27%), followed by 26%–50% (22.73%). Notably, 18.18% of students spend more than half of their daily budget on travel, whereas 16.67% spend nothing (mostly students living within 5 km of the university) and 15.15% spend less than 10%.


#### How often students feel unsafe

```{r v-feel-unsafe}
res <- one_var("feel_unsafe", chart = "bar")
res$table
res$plot
```

Most students rarely (35.61%) or never (27.27%) feel unsafe while commuting. However, 30.30% sometimes feel unsafe and 6.82% often do, so 37.12% of students feel unsafe at least some of the time.


### 1.1.3 Commute experience and wellbeing

#### C1 Stressed – relaxed

```{r v-stressed-relaxed, fig.width = 9}
res <- one_var("stressed_relaxed", chart = "bar")
res$table
res$plot
```

Responses lean towards the stressed side of the scale. About half of the students (52.27%) felt at least slightly stressed during the commute (−1 to −3), compared with 26.52% who felt relaxed (+1 to +3) and 21.21% who felt neither. The most common answer was 'slightly stressed' (29.55%).


#### C2 Worried – confident

```{r v-worried-confident, fig.width = 9}
res <- one_var("worried_confident", chart = "bar")
res$table
res$plot
```

The most common response was neutral (31.82%). Still, 39.39% of students felt at least slightly worried, compared with 28.79% who felt confident. The distribution is therefore centred near the middle of the scale, with a moderate lean towards worry.


#### C3 Hurried – calm

```{r v-hurried-calm, fig.width = 9}
res <- one_var("hurried_calm", chart = "bar")
res$table
res$plot
```

This item leans most strongly to the negative side of the three: 58.33% of students felt at least slightly hurried, while only 21.21% felt calm and 20.45% felt neither. 'Slightly hurried' was the most frequent answer (30.30%).


#### C4 Stress felt these days

```{r v-stress-these-days}
res <- one_var("stress_these_days", chart = "bar")
res$table
res$plot
```

Most students report low to moderate general stress: 38.64% feel stressed 'only a little' and 34.09% 'to some extent'. Only 9.09% feel stressed 'rather much' or 'very much', while 18.18% do not feel stressed at all.


#### Sleep quality last night

```{r v-sleep-quality}
res <- one_var("sleep_quality", chart = "bar")
res$table
res$plot
```

Sleep quality on the previous night was most often average (42.42%). One-third of the students (33.33%) slept well (good or very good), while 24.24% slept poorly (poor or very poor).


#### Academic workload pressure

```{r v-workload-pressure}
res <- one_var("workload_pressure", chart = "bar")
res$table
res$plot
```

Almost half of the students (48.48%) rated their academic workload pressure as moderate. A substantial 40.91% rated it high or very high, while only 10.61% rated it low or very low.


#### Crowding on bus/train

Only bus and train users answered this question; blanks are excluded.

```{r v-crowding}
res <- one_var("crowding", chart = "bar")
res$table
res$plot
```

Of the 79 bus and train users, 37.97% described their vehicle as very crowded and 6.33% as extremely crowded, so 44.30% travelled in heavily crowded conditions. A further 30.38% reported moderate crowding (all seats taken), while only 25.32% found the vehicle not or slightly crowded.


#### Weather made commute harder

```{r v-weather-impact}
res <- one_var("weather_impact", chart = "bar")
res$table
res$plot
```

Weather made the commute harder for most students: 29.55% said it made the commute moderately harder, 19.70% very much harder and 11.36% extremely harder. Only 14.39% said the weather did not make the commute harder at all.


#### Stress level

```{r v-stress-level}
res <- one_var("stress_level", chart = "bar")
res$table
res$plot
```

Based on the commute stress score, most students (64.39%, 85) are at a moderate stress level. Almost a quarter (24.24%, 32) are highly stressed, while only 11.36% (15) have low stress. Highly stressed students therefore outnumber low-stress students by about two to one.


## 1.2 Two qualitative variables

Each table shows the count and the **row percentage** (percentage within each
group of the first variable). The bars in each cluster add up to 100%. Small
categories are merged (see the `merged-data` chunk). Crowding is compared for
bus and train users only.


### 1.2.1 Stress level compared with other variables


#### Stress level by gender

```{r tw-gender-x-stress-level, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 5}
res <- two_way(row = "gender", col = "stress_level")
res$table
res$plot
```

Female students show higher commute stress than male students. 31.1% of female students are at the high stress level, compared with 18.3% of male students, while low stress is much more common among males (16.9%) than females (4.9%). The share at the moderate level is almost identical for both groups (64.8% and 63.9%).


#### Stress level by one-way distance to university

```{r tw-distance-x-stress-level, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 5}
res <- two_way(row = "distance", col = "stress_level")
res$table
res$plot
```

Stress rises steadily with distance. The share of highly stressed students increases from 11.1% among those living less than 5 km away to 20.5% (5–14 km), 34.1% (15–29 km) and 38.5% (30 km or more). At the same time, the share with low stress falls from 22.2% to 0.0%. Living further from the university is therefore associated with higher commute stress.


#### Stress level by main transport mode

```{r tw-main-mode-x-stress-level, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 5}
res <- two_way(row = "main_mode", col = "stress_level")
res$table
res$plot
```

Stress differs clearly by main mode. Train (50.0%) and bus users (32.9%) have the highest shares of high stress, whereas only 7.4% of private-vehicle users and 5.6% of those who walk or cycle are highly stressed. Low stress is most common among private-vehicle users (33.3%) and almost absent among bus users (1.4%). Only 6 students use the train and 8 use three-wheelers or taxis, so the percentages for these groups should be interpreted with caution.


#### Stress level by mode from home to main vehicle

```{r tw-access-mode-x-stress-level, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 5}
res <- two_way(row = "access_mode", col = "stress_level")
res$table
res$plot
```

Students with direct access to their main vehicle have the lowest stress: only 9.1% are highly stressed and 25.0% have low stress. High stress is more common among those dropped off by someone (42.9%), those who walk to their main vehicle (32.2%) and those who take a three-wheeler (30.0%). The direct-access group consists mainly of private-vehicle users and students who walk or cycle the whole way, which helps explain its lower stress.


#### Stress level by mode from main vehicle to university gate

```{r tw-egress-mode-x-stress-level, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 5}
res <- two_way(row = "egress_mode", col = "stress_level")
res$table
res$plot
```

A similar pattern appears for the last stretch to the gate. Students dropped directly at the gate have the lowest stress (6.8% high, 25.0% low), while 36.4% of those taking a three-wheeler and 29.7% of those walking from their vehicle are highly stressed. Both students who take a bus for the last stretch are highly stressed, but this group is too small (n = 2) to draw conclusions.


#### Stress level by seat availability

```{r tw-seat-x-stress-level, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 5}
res <- two_way(row = "seat", col = "stress_level")
res$table
res$plot
```

Students for whom a seat is not applicable (mainly those who walk, cycle or travel by private vehicle) have the lowest stress (7.9% high, 23.7% low). Among public-transport users, the share of highly stressed students is similar for those who usually stand (33.3%) and those who usually get a seat (29.5%), although no student who stands has low stress. Getting a seat therefore does not, by itself, protect students from high stress.


#### Stress level by one-way trip time

```{r tw-trip-time-x-stress-level, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 5}
res <- two_way(row = "trip_time", col = "stress_level")
res$table
res$plot
```

Trip time shows the clearest relationship with stress. Low stress is found mainly among students whose trips take under 30 minutes (29.5%) and disappears completely for trips of one hour or more. The share of highly stressed students rises from 6.8% (under 30 minutes) to 20.0% (30–59 minutes), 25.0% (1 to 1½ hours) and 60.9% (1½ to 2 hours). The over-2-hours group is small (n = 6), so its lower value (33.3%) should be interpreted with caution.


#### Stress level by waiting time for vehicle

```{r tw-wait-time-x-stress-level, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 5}
res <- two_way(row = "wait_time", col = "stress_level")
res$table
res$plot
```

Stress increases with waiting time. Only 7.0% of students who do not wait are highly stressed, compared with 16.0% of those who wait under 5 minutes, 33.3% of those who wait 5–15 minutes and 56.2% of those who wait 15 minutes or more. Conversely, low stress falls from 20.9% to 0.0%.


#### Stress level by departure time

```{r tw-departure-time-x-stress-level, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 5}
res <- two_way(row = "departure_time", col = "stress_level")
res$table
res$plot
```

Students who leave earlier are more stressed. Nearly half of those who leave before 6:00 am (46.7%) are highly stressed, compared with 27.5% of those leaving between 6:00 and 6:59 am, 19.2% between 7:00 and 7:59 am and 7.1% at 8:00 am or later. Early departure largely reflects longer distances (see Section 1.2.2).


#### Stress level by how often students feel unsafe

```{r tw-feel-unsafe-x-stress-level, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 5}
res <- two_way(row = "feel_unsafe", col = "stress_level")
res$table
res$plot
```

Feeling unsafe is closely linked to stress. The share of highly stressed students rises from 5.6% among those who never feel unsafe to 23.4% (rarely), 35.0% (sometimes) and 55.6% (often). Low stress is found only among students who never or rarely feel unsafe (27.8% and 10.6%).


#### Stress level by sleep quality last night

```{r tw-sleep-quality-x-stress-level, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 5}
res <- two_way(row = "sleep_quality", col = "stress_level")
res$table
res$plot
```

There is no clear pattern between sleep quality and stress level. High stress is somewhat more common after poor or very poor sleep (37.0% and 40.0%) than after average or good sleep (21.4% and 14.3%), but 33.3% of those who slept very well are also highly stressed. The very poor (n = 5) and very good (n = 9) groups are small, so their percentages are unstable.


#### Stress level by academic workload pressure

```{r tw-workload-pressure-x-stress-level, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 5}
res <- two_way(row = "workload_pressure", col = "stress_level")
res$table
res$plot
```

Academic workload pressure does not show a consistent relationship with commute stress. The share of highly stressed students is 35.7% in the low workload group, 17.2% for moderate, 33.3% for high and 22.2% for very high, with no steady upward or downward trend. Commute stress therefore appears to be largely independent of academic workload.


#### Stress level by crowding on bus/train

```{r tw-crowding-x-stress-level, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 5}
res <- two_way(row = "crowding", col = "stress_level")
res$table
res$plot
```

Among bus and train users, stress increases with crowding. Only 10.0% of those in not or slightly crowded vehicles are highly stressed, compared with 29.2% in moderately crowded and 53.3% in very crowded vehicles. The extremely crowded group (40.0% high stress) contains only 5 students, so this value is less reliable.


#### Stress level by weather made commute harder

```{r tw-weather-impact-x-stress-level, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 5}
res <- two_way(row = "weather_impact", col = "stress_level")
res$table
res$plot
```

Stress tends to be higher when the weather makes the commute harder. The share of highly stressed students increases from 10.5% (not at all) and 15.2% (slightly) to 25.6% (moderately) and 38.5% (very much). In the 'extremely' group, both high stress (33.3%) and low stress (26.7%) are relatively common, so the pattern is less clear at the top of the scale.


### 1.2.2 Distance compared with other variables


#### Main transport mode by one-way distance to university

```{r tw-distance-x-main-mode, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 5}
res <- two_way(row = "distance", col = "main_mode")
res$table
res$plot
```

The main mode changes with distance. Half of the students living less than 5 km away walk or cycle (50.0%), but no student living further away does. For distances of 5 km or more, the bus is the dominant mode (65.9%–69.2%), and private vehicles are used by 25.0%–30.8% of students up to 29 km. The train is used only for longer trips, by 23.1% of students travelling 30 km or more.


#### Number of vehicle changes by one-way distance to university

```{r tw-distance-x-vehicle-changes, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 5}
res <- two_way(row = "distance", col = "vehicle_changes")
res$table
res$plot
```

The number of vehicle changes rises sharply with distance. Most students living less than 5 km away (77.8%) do not change vehicles, but this falls to 46.2% (5–14 km), 34.1% (15–29 km) and only 7.7% (30 km or more). Among students travelling 30 km or more, 69.2% change vehicles at least twice.


#### Seat availability by one-way distance to university

```{r tw-distance-x-seat, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 5}
res <- two_way(row = "distance", col = "seat")
res$table
res$plot
```

Students living close to the university are most often in the 'not applicable' group (55.6%), as many of them walk or cycle. For distances of 5 km or more, between 48.7% and 54.5% usually get a seat, while 25.0%–33.3% usually stand. The share who stand does not rise steadily with distance.


#### Late arrivals (15+ minutes) by one-way distance to university

```{r tw-distance-x-late-arrivals, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 5}
res <- two_way(row = "distance", col = "late_arrivals")
res$table
res$plot
```

Late arrivals do not increase with distance. Students living less than 5 km away are late two or more days a week (36.1%) about as often as those living 5–14 km (33.3%) and 15–29 km (29.5%) away. Students travelling 30 km or more are the least often late (7.7% late two or more days a week), possibly because they leave much earlier.


#### One-way trip time by one-way distance to university

```{r tw-distance-x-trip-time, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 5}
res <- two_way(row = "distance", col = "trip_time")
res$table
res$plot
```

As expected, trip time increases with distance. Almost all students living less than 5 km away (88.9%) arrive in under 30 minutes, while most of those living 5–14 km away take 30–59 minutes (51.3%). At 15–29 km, 70.5% need an hour or more, and among those travelling 30 km or more, 84.6% take more than 1½ hours.


#### Share of daily budget spent on travel by one-way distance to university

```{r tw-distance-x-travel-budget, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 5}
res <- two_way(row = "distance", col = "travel_budget")
res$table
res$plot
```

The share of the daily budget spent on travel rises with distance. More than half of the students living less than 5 km away (52.8%) spend nothing on travel, whereas more than half of those travelling 30 km or more (53.8%) spend over 50% of their daily budget. Among students living 15–29 km away, 61.4% spend more than a quarter of their budget on travel.


#### Departure time by one-way distance to university

```{r tw-distance-x-departure-time, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 5}
res <- two_way(row = "distance", col = "departure_time")
res$table
res$plot
```

Students who live further away leave home earlier. Most students within 5 km leave between 7:00 and 7:59 am (72.2%), while most of those living 15–29 km away leave between 6:00 and 6:59 am (65.9%). More than half of those travelling 30 km or more (53.8%) leave before 6:00 am.


#### Crowding on bus/train by one-way distance to university

```{r tw-distance-x-crowding, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 5}
res <- two_way(row = "distance", col = "crowding")
res$table
res$plot
```

Among the 79 bus and train users, crowding tends to increase with distance. The share travelling in very crowded vehicles rises from 11.1% (less than 5 km) to 34.6% (5–14 km), 40.6% (15–29 km) and 58.3% (30 km or more). Only 9 bus or train users live within 5 km, so the percentages for that group should be read with caution.


#### Weather made commute harder by one-way distance to university

```{r tw-distance-x-weather-impact, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 5}
res <- two_way(row = "distance", col = "weather_impact")
res$table
res$plot
```

The effect of weather is broadly similar across distances. Weather made the commute very much or extremely harder for 25.0% of students living less than 5 km away, 33.3% at 5–14 km, 31.8% at 15–29 km and 38.5% at 30 km or more. Students living nearby are the most likely to say the weather had no effect (22.2%), but 22.2% of them also found it extremely hard, probably because many of them walk or cycle.


### 1.2.3 Main transport mode compared with other variables


#### Mode from home to main vehicle by main transport mode

```{r tw-main-mode-x-access-mode, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 5}
res <- two_way(row = "main_mode", col = "access_mode")
res$table
res$plot
```

How students reach their main vehicle depends on the mode. Most bus users (71.2%) walk to the bus, while most private-vehicle users (74.1%) and all students who walk or cycle (100.0%) have direct access. Three-wheeler or taxi users also mostly have direct access (62.5%), whereas train users walk, are dropped off or take a bus to the station (33.3% each).


#### Mode from main vehicle to university gate by main transport mode

```{r tw-main-mode-x-egress-mode, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 5}
res <- two_way(row = "main_mode", col = "egress_mode")
res$table
res$plot
```

For the last stretch to the university gate, most bus users walk (71.2%) and 23.3% take a three-wheeler. Most private-vehicle users (70.4%) and all students who walk or cycle reach the gate directly. Train users either walk (50.0%) or take a three-wheeler (50.0%) from the station. Public-transport users therefore usually need an extra leg at the end of their journey.


#### Seat availability by main transport mode

```{r tw-main-mode-x-seat, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 5}
res <- two_way(row = "main_mode", col = "seat")
res$table
res$plot
```

Among bus users, 58.9% usually get a seat but 39.7% usually stand. Train users stand even more often (66.7%), although this group is small (n = 6). Private-vehicle and three-wheeler users either get a seat or found the question not applicable, and the question does not apply to students who walk or cycle.


#### Late arrivals (15+ minutes) by main transport mode

```{r tw-main-mode-x-late-arrivals, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 5}
res <- two_way(row = "main_mode", col = "late_arrivals")
res$table
res$plot
```

Late arrivals occur with every mode. About one-third of bus users (31.5%) and train users (33.3%) are late two or more days a week, and the share is highest among students who walk or cycle (44.4%). Three-wheeler or taxi users are the most punctual: 62.5% are never late and none are late two or more days a week.


#### One-way trip time by main transport mode

```{r tw-main-mode-x-trip-time, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 5}
res <- two_way(row = "main_mode", col = "trip_time")
res$table
res$plot
```

Trip time differs strongly by mode. All students who walk or cycle arrive in under 30 minutes, and 92.6% of private-vehicle users take less than an hour. In contrast, 61.6% of bus users and 83.3% of train users travel for an hour or more each way, and 8.2% of bus users travel for over 2 hours.


#### Waiting time for vehicle by main transport mode

```{r tw-main-mode-x-wait-time, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 5}
res <- two_way(row = "main_mode", col = "wait_time")
res$table
res$plot
```

Waiting is mainly a public-transport issue. Most private-vehicle users (81.5%) and all students who walk or cycle do not wait. More than half of bus users (53.4%) wait 5–15 minutes and 19.2% wait 15 minutes or more, while 83.3% of train users wait 5–15 minutes.


#### Departure time by main transport mode

```{r tw-main-mode-x-departure-time, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 5}
res <- two_way(row = "main_mode", col = "departure_time")
res$table
res$plot
```

Bus and train users leave home earliest: 64.4% of bus users and all train users leave before 7:00 am. Private-vehicle users most often leave between 7:00 and 7:59 am (48.1%), and all students who walk or cycle leave at 7:00 am or later.


#### How often students feel unsafe by main transport mode

```{r tw-main-mode-x-feel-unsafe, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 5}
res <- two_way(row = "main_mode", col = "feel_unsafe")
res$table
res$plot
```

Feeling unsafe is more common on public transport. Among train users, 83.3% sometimes feel unsafe, and 42.4% of bus users feel unsafe sometimes or often. In contrast, 66.7% of students who walk or cycle and 37.0% of private-vehicle users never feel unsafe.


#### Crowding on bus/train by main transport mode

```{r tw-main-mode-x-crowding, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 5}
res <- two_way(row = "main_mode", col = "crowding")
res$table
res$plot
```

Only bus and train users answered this question. All six train users described their train as very crowded. Bus users reported a wider range: 39.7% found the bus very or extremely crowded, 32.9% moderately crowded and 27.4% not or slightly crowded.


#### Weather made commute harder by main transport mode

```{r tw-main-mode-x-weather-impact, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 5}
res <- two_way(row = "main_mode", col = "weather_impact")
res$table
res$plot
```

Weather affects bus users the most: 37.0% of them said it made the commute very much or extremely harder. The share is lower for private-vehicle users (25.9%) and for those who walk or cycle (22.2%), and one-third (33.3%) of students who walk or cycle said the weather had no effect at all.


### 1.2.4 Residence compared with other variables


#### Stress level by residence during semester

```{r tw-residence-x-stress-level, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 5}
res <- two_way(row = "residence", col = "stress_level")
res$table
res$plot
```

Students living at home are the most stressed: 27.9% of them are at the high stress level, compared with 10.0% of those in boarding places and 12.5% of those in the university hostel. Low stress is most common among hostel residents (50.0%). The hostel group contains only 8 students, so its percentages should be interpreted with caution.


#### Main transport mode by residence during semester

```{r tw-residence-x-main-mode, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 5}
res <- two_way(row = "residence", col = "main_mode")
res$table
res$plot
```

Residence strongly shapes the mode of travel. Most students living at home travel by bus (64.4%) or private vehicle (23.1%), and none walk or cycle. In contrast, 70.0% of boarders and 50.0% of hostel residents walk or cycle to the university.


#### One-way distance to university by residence during semester

```{r tw-residence-x-distance, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 5}
res <- two_way(row = "residence", col = "distance")
res$table
res$plot
```

Boarders and hostel residents live much closer to the university: 90.0% of boarders and 62.5% of hostel residents live less than 5 km away, compared with only 12.5% of students living at home. More than half of the students living at home (52.9%) travel 15 km or more.


## 1.3 Three qualitative variables

Trip time is grouped into three classes and main mode into two
(see the `merged-data` chunk) so that each group still has enough students.

### Stress level by trip time and gender

```{r th-trip-gender, fig.width = 10, fig.height = 5}
res <- three_way(row = "trip_time3", panel = "gender", col = "stress_level")
res$table
res$plot
```

When trip time is taken into account, the gender difference appears mainly for shorter trips. For trips under one hour, female students are more often highly stressed than male students (11.1% vs 3.8% for under 30 minutes, and 35.3% vs 5.6% for 30–59 minutes). For trips of one hour or more, the share of highly stressed students is almost the same for both genders (40.7% for males and 42.3% for females). Long trips are therefore stressful regardless of gender.

### Stress level by trip time and seat availability (bus and train users)

Only bus and train users who usually get a seat or usually stand are included.

```{r th-trip-seat, fig.width = 10, fig.height = 5}
bus_train <- data_m %>% filter(mode2 == "Bus / train", seat != "Not applicable")
res <- three_way(row = "trip_time3", panel = "seat", col = "stress_level", df = bus_train)
res$table
res$plot
```

Among bus and train users, the share of highly stressed students rises with trip time both for those who get a seat and for those who stand. For trips of one hour or more, 43.8% of students who usually get a seat are highly stressed, which is similar to the 41.2% of those who usually stand. Trip duration therefore matters more than having a seat. The groups with trips under one hour are small (4–12 students), so their percentages should be treated with caution.

### Stress level by distance and main transport mode

```{r th-distance-mode, fig.width = 10, fig.height = 5}
res <- three_way(row = "distance2", panel = "mode2", col = "stress_level")
res$table
res$plot
```

Within each mode group, stress is higher for longer distances. Among bus and train users, high stress rises from 28.6% (under 15 km) to 38.6% (15 km or more). Among private or hired vehicle users, it rises from 4.5% to 23.1%, while low stress falls from 40.9% to 15.4%. At both distances, public-transport users are more often highly stressed than private or hired vehicle users, so both mode and distance are related to stress. All students who walk or cycle live under 15 km away, and only 5.6% of them are highly stressed.


# 2. Data description

## 2.1 One quantitative variable: stress score

### Summary measures and skewness

The score is recalculated from C1–C3 without rounding, so quartiles and outlier
fences are exact. Quartiles use the same method as Minitab (`type = 6`). Skewness is the adjusted
Fisher–Pearson coefficient (as in Minitab and Excel `SKEW`):

* between −0.5 and +0.5: approximately symmetric → use **mean, SD and variance**
* below −0.5: negatively skewed; above +0.5: positively skewed → use **median and IQR**

```{r score-summary}
s <- -rowSums(items) / 3     # exact stress score (items = C1-C3, from Section 0)
n <- length(s)

q   <- quantile(s, c(0.25, 0.50, 0.75), type = 6)
iqr <- unname(q[3] - q[1])

skewness_G1 <- function(x) {
  n  <- length(x)
  m2 <- mean((x - mean(x))^2)
  m3 <- mean((x - mean(x))^3)
  (m3 / m2^1.5) * sqrt(n * (n - 1)) / (n - 2)
}
skew <- skewness_G1(s)

shape <- if (skew > 0.5) "positively skewed" else if (skew < -0.5) "negatively skewed" else "approximately symmetric"

five_num <- data.frame(
  Measure = c("n", "Minimum", "Q1", "Median (Q2)", "Q3", "Maximum", "Skewness"),
  Value   = round(c(n, min(s), q[1], q[2], q[3], max(s), skew), 3) + 0)
add_table(five_num, "2.1 Stress score: summary measures")
kable(five_num, align = "lr")
```

Skewness = **`r round(skew, 3)`**, so the stress score distribution is
**`r shape`**.

```{r score-centre-spread}
# The appropriate centre and spread are chosen automatically from the skewness
if (shape == "approximately symmetric") {
  centre_spread <- data.frame(
    Measure = c("Mean", "Standard deviation", "Variance"),
    Value   = round(c(mean(s), sd(s), var(s)), 3))
} else {
  centre_spread <- data.frame(
    Measure = c("Median", "Interquartile range (IQR = Q3 − Q1)"),
    Value   = round(c(q[2], iqr), 3))
}
add_table(centre_spread, "2.1 Stress score: centre and spread")
kable(centre_spread, align = "lr")
```

The stress score ranges from −3.00 to +3.00, with a median of 0.33, meaning that the typical student feels slightly more stressed than relaxed during the commute. The middle 50% of students have scores between −0.33 (Q1) and 1.00 (Q3), giving an interquartile range of 1.33. The skewness coefficient is −0.575, so the distribution is moderately negatively skewed; the median and IQR are therefore used instead of the mean and standard deviation.

### Histogram

Each bar is one possible score (scores move in steps of 1/3). Bar colours show the
stress level; the dashed lines mark the cut-offs at −1 and +1.

```{r score-histogram, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 5}
h <- data.frame(score = round(s, 2)) %>%
  count(score) %>%
  mutate(pct   = 100 * n / sum(n),
         level = factor(case_when(score > 1 ~ "High", score < -1 ~ "Low", TRUE ~ "Moderate"),
                        levels = c("Low", "Moderate", "High")))

p_hist <- ggplot(h, aes(x = score, y = n, fill = level)) +
  geom_col(width = 1/3 - 0.02) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.1f%%", pct)), vjust = -0.4, family = FONT, size = 3.2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(-1, 1), linetype = "dashed", colour = "#52514e", linewidth = 0.4) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = palette_for("stress_level", 3), name = "Stress level", drop = FALSE) +
  scale_x_continuous(name = "Stress score (-3 = very relaxed, +3 = very stressed)",
                     breaks = -3:3, limits = c(-3.3, 3.3)) +
  scale_y_continuous(name = "Number of students", expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.12))) +
  theme_report()
save_fig(p_hist, "2.1_stress_score_histogram", width = 9, height = 5)
p_hist
```

The most common score is 0.00 (19 students), followed by 1.00 (17) and 0.67 (16), and 64.39% of the scores fall between −1 and +1 (moderate stress). The distribution has a longer tail to the left, towards the relaxed end, which confirms the negative skewness. More students fall above +1 (high stress, 24.24%) than below −1 (low stress, 11.36%).

### Box plot

The box runs from Q1 to Q3 with the median (Q2) inside. The whiskers reach the
smallest and largest scores that are **not** outliers. Outliers are scores more
than 1.5 × IQR below Q1 or above Q3.

```{r score-boxplot, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 4}
lower_fence <- q[1] - 1.5 * iqr
upper_fence <- q[3] + 1.5 * iqr
tol <- 1e-9                                   # a score exactly on a fence is not an outlier
is_out   <- s < lower_fence - tol | s > upper_fence + tol
whisk_lo <- min(s[!is_out])
whisk_hi <- max(s[!is_out])
outliers <- s[is_out]

box_df <- data.frame(x = 1, ymin = whisk_lo, lower = q[1], middle = q[2],
                     upper = q[3], ymax = whisk_hi)
out_df <- as.data.frame(table(score = round(outliers, 2)))
out_df$score <- as.numeric(as.character(out_df$score))

marks <- data.frame(
  y     = c(whisk_lo, q[1], q[2], q[3], whisk_hi),
  label = paste(c("Min =", "Q1 =", "Q2 =", "Q3 =", "Max ="),
                sprintf("%.2f", round(c(whisk_lo, q[1], q[2], q[3], whisk_hi), 2) + 0)),
  x     = c(1.32, 0.68, 1.32, 0.68, 1.32))     # alternate above / below the box

p_box <- ggplot() +
  geom_boxplot(data = box_df, stat = "identity", width = 0.4, colour = "#0b0b0b",
               aes(x = x, ymin = ymin, lower = lower, middle = middle, upper = upper,
                   ymax = ymax, fill = "Middle 50% (Q1 to Q3)")) +
  geom_text(data = marks, aes(x = x, y = y, label = label), family = FONT, size = 4.2) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = "#86b6ef", name = NULL) +
  scale_y_continuous(name = "Stress score (-3 = very relaxed, +3 = very stressed)",
                     breaks = -3:3, limits = c(-3.2, 3.2)) +
  scale_x_continuous(name = NULL, breaks = NULL, limits = c(0.55, 1.45)) +
  coord_flip() +
  theme_report() +
  theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.major.x = element_line(colour = "#e1e0d9", linewidth = 0.3),
        axis.line.y = element_blank())

if (nrow(out_df) > 0) {
  p_box <- p_box +
    geom_point(data = out_df, aes(x = 1, y = score, shape = "Outlier"), size = 3) +
    geom_text(data = out_df,
              aes(x = rep(c(1.12, 0.88), length.out = nrow(out_df)), y = score,
                  label = sprintf("%.2f (n = %d)", score, Freq)),
              family = FONT, size = 3.6) +
    scale_shape_manual(values = 8, name = NULL)
}
save_fig(p_box, "2.1_stress_score_boxplot", width = 9, height = 4)
p_box

outlier_tab <- if (nrow(out_df) > 0) {
  setNames(out_df, c("Outlier score", "Number of students"))
} else data.frame(Note = "No outliers")
add_table(outlier_tab, "2.1 Stress score: outliers")
kable(outlier_tab, align = "rr")
```

Lower fence = `r round(lower_fence, 2)`, upper fence = `r round(upper_fence, 2)`.

The box is centred on the median (0.33), and both whiskers have the same length (2.00 units, from −2.33 to −0.33 and from 1.00 to 3.00). The negative skewness therefore comes mainly from five low outliers: three students scored −3.00 and two scored −2.67, meaning they felt very relaxed, confident and calm. These are genuine responses rather than errors, so they are kept in the analysis. A score of −2.33 lies exactly on the lower fence and is therefore not treated as an outlier, and there are no high outliers.


# 3. Relationships between variables

A Pearson correlation matrix only measures **straight-line relationships between
numeric variables**, so it is not suitable here. This section uses measures made
for categorical data:

* **Spearman's rho** (3.1): for ordinal variables and the stress score. It
  measures any relationship that keeps going in one direction (as one goes up,
  the other tends to go up, or down). It runs from −1 to +1.
* **Cramér's V** (3.2, 3.3): for any two categorical variables, nominal or
  ordinal. It is based on the chi-square test and runs from 0 (no association)
  to 1 (perfect association). It has no sign, so it shows strength only. The
  bias-corrected version is used, because the ordinary version is too high in
  small samples with many categories. Merged categories (`data_m`) are used.

Rough guide to strength (both measures): below 0.10 negligible, 0.10–0.29 weak,
0.30–0.49 moderate, 0.50 or above strong.

```{r assoc-setup}
short <- c(
  days_per_week = "Days per week", faculty = "Faculty", study_year = "Year of study",
  gender = "Gender", residence = "Residence", distance = "Distance",
  main_mode = "Main mode", vehicle_changes = "Vehicle changes",
  access_mode = "Access mode", egress_mode = "Egress mode", seat = "Seat",
  late_arrivals = "Late arrivals", trip_time = "Trip time", wait_time = "Waiting time",
  departure_time = "Departure time", travel_budget = "Travel budget",
  feel_unsafe = "Feel unsafe", stress_these_days = "Stress these days (C4)",
  sleep_quality = "Sleep quality", workload_pressure = "Workload pressure",
  crowding = "Crowding", weather_impact = "Weather impact",
  stress_level = "Stress level", stress_score = "Stress score")

ord_vars <- c("days_per_week", "study_year", "distance", "vehicle_changes",
              "late_arrivals", "trip_time", "wait_time", "departure_time",
              "travel_budget", "feel_unsafe", "stress_these_days", "sleep_quality",
              "workload_pressure", "crowding", "weather_impact")
cat_vars <- c("faculty", "gender", "residence", "main_mode", "access_mode",
              "egress_mode", "seat", ord_vars, "stress_level")

# Lower-triangle heat map used in 3.1 and 3.2
heatmap_plot <- function(mat, pmat, fill_name, diverging = TRUE) {
  vars <- colnames(mat)
  hd <- expand.grid(x = vars, y = vars, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  hd$value <- mat[cbind(hd$y, hd$x)]
  hd$p     <- pmat[cbind(hd$y, hd$x)]
  hd <- hd[match(hd$x, vars) < match(hd$y, vars), ]          # lower triangle only
  hd$label <- paste0(sprintf("%.2f", hd$value), ifelse(hd$p < 0.05, "*", ""))
  hd$x <- factor(short[hd$x], levels = short[vars])
  hd$y <- factor(short[hd$y], levels = rev(short[vars]))
  scale_fill <- if (diverging) {
    scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#eb6834", mid = "#f7f6f2", high = "#2a78d6",
                         midpoint = 0, limits = c(-1, 1), name = fill_name)
  } else {
    scale_fill_gradient(low = "#f7f6f2", high = "#184f95", limits = c(0, 1), name = fill_name)
  }
  ggplot(hd, aes(x = x, y = y, fill = value)) +
    geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 0.6) +
    geom_text(aes(label = label, colour = abs(value) > 0.6), family = FONT, size = 3) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = "black", `TRUE` = "white"), guide = "none") +
    scale_fill +
    scale_x_discrete(name = NULL, position = "bottom") +
    scale_y_discrete(name = NULL) +
    theme_report() +
    theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),
          panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(), axis.line = element_blank(),
          axis.ticks = element_blank())
}

# Bias-corrected Cramér's V (Bergsma, 2013) and a Monte Carlo chi-square p-value
cramer_v <- function(x, y) {
  ok <- !is.na(x) & !is.na(y)
  tb <- table(droplevels(x[ok]), droplevels(y[ok]))
  n  <- sum(tb); r <- nrow(tb); k <- ncol(tb)
  chi   <- suppressWarnings(chisq.test(tb, correct = FALSE)$statistic)
  phi2c <- max(0, chi / n - (k - 1) * (r - 1) / (n - 1))
  rc <- r - (r - 1)^2 / (n - 1); kc <- k - (k - 1)^2 / (n - 1)
  unname(sqrt(phi2c / min(kc - 1, rc - 1)))
}
chisq_p <- function(x, y) {
  ok <- !is.na(x) & !is.na(y)
  tb <- table(droplevels(x[ok]), droplevels(y[ok]))
  chisq.test(tb, simulate.p.value = TRUE, B = 5000)$p.value   # exact-style p-value, fine for small cells
}
```

## 3.1 Spearman correlation: ordinal variables and stress score

Each ordinal variable is turned into its rank order (1, 2, 3, ...). Blue means a
positive relationship and orange a negative one; * marks p < 0.05. C1–C3 and
stress level are left out because the stress score is built from them.

```{r spearman-heatmap, fig.width = 11, fig.height = 9}
num <- as.data.frame(lapply(data[ord_vars], as.numeric))
num$stress_score <- -rowSums(items) / 3

vars <- names(num)
sp_mat <- cor(num, method = "spearman", use = "pairwise.complete.obs")
sp_p   <- matrix(NA, length(vars), length(vars), dimnames = list(vars, vars))
for (i in vars) for (j in vars) if (i != j) {
  sp_p[i, j] <- suppressWarnings(cor.test(num[[i]], num[[j]], method = "spearman",
                                          exact = FALSE)$p.value)
}

p_sp <- heatmap_plot(sp_mat, sp_p, "Spearman's rho")
save_fig(p_sp, "3.1_spearman_heatmap", width = 11, height = 9)
p_sp

sp_tab <- data.frame(round(sp_mat, 3), check.names = FALSE)
names(sp_tab) <- short[names(sp_tab)]
sp_tab <- cbind(Variable = short[rownames(sp_mat)], sp_tab)
add_table(sp_tab, "3.1 Spearman correlation matrix")

# Correlation of each variable with the stress score, strongest first
with_score <- data.frame(Variable = short[vars[vars != "stress_score"]],
                         rho = sp_mat[vars != "stress_score", "stress_score"],
                         p   = sp_p[vars != "stress_score", "stress_score"])
with_score <- with_score[order(-abs(with_score$rho)), ]
with_score$rho <- round(with_score$rho, 3); with_score$p <- signif(with_score$p, 3)
names(with_score) <- c("Variable", "Spearman's rho with stress score", "p-value")
rownames(with_score) <- NULL
add_table(with_score, "3.1 Spearman correlation with stress score")
kable(with_score)
```

Several travel variables have moderate positive correlations with the stress score: trip time (ρ = 0.53), waiting time (0.47), feeling unsafe (0.38), distance (0.38), vehicle changes (0.37) and travel budget (0.33), all with p < 0.001. Departure time is negatively correlated with stress (ρ = −0.28, p = 0.001), so students who leave later are less stressed. Crowding (0.24), weather impact (0.22), general stress (C4, 0.20) and sleep quality (−0.18) have weak but significant correlations, while late arrivals, days per week, year of study and workload pressure are not significantly related to the stress score. The travel variables are also strongly correlated with one another, especially distance and trip time (ρ = 0.80), so their relationships with stress overlap.

## 3.2 Cramér's V: all categorical variables

* marks a significant chi-square test (p < 0.05, Monte Carlo p-value). Darker
cells mean a stronger association.

```{r cramer-heatmap, fig.width = 12, fig.height = 10.5}
set.seed(2026)
cv_mat <- matrix(1, length(cat_vars), length(cat_vars), dimnames = list(cat_vars, cat_vars))
cv_p   <- matrix(0, length(cat_vars), length(cat_vars), dimnames = list(cat_vars, cat_vars))
for (a in seq_along(cat_vars)) for (b in seq_along(cat_vars)) if (a < b) {
  i <- cat_vars[a]; j <- cat_vars[b]
  cv_mat[i, j] <- cv_mat[j, i] <- cramer_v(data_m[[i]], data_m[[j]])
  cv_p[i, j]   <- cv_p[j, i]   <- chisq_p(data_m[[i]], data_m[[j]])
}

p_cv <- heatmap_plot(cv_mat, cv_p, "Cramér's V", diverging = FALSE)
save_fig(p_cv, "3.2_cramers_v_heatmap", width = 12, height = 10.5)
p_cv

cv_tab <- data.frame(round(cv_mat, 3), check.names = FALSE)
names(cv_tab) <- short[names(cv_tab)]
cv_tab <- cbind(Variable = short[rownames(cv_mat)], cv_tab)
add_table(cv_tab, "3.2 Cramér's V matrix")

# Strongest pairs (excluding stress level, shown in 3.3)
pairs <- which(upper.tri(cv_mat), arr.ind = TRUE)
top_pairs <- data.frame(`Variable 1` = short[rownames(cv_mat)[pairs[, 1]]],
                        `Variable 2` = short[colnames(cv_mat)[pairs[, 2]]],
                        `Cramér's V` = round(cv_mat[pairs], 3),
                        `p-value` = signif(cv_p[pairs], 3), check.names = FALSE)
top_pairs <- top_pairs[top_pairs$`Variable 1` != "Stress level" & top_pairs$`Variable 2` != "Stress level", ]
top_pairs <- head(top_pairs[order(-top_pairs$`Cramér's V`), ], 10)
rownames(top_pairs) <- NULL
add_table(top_pairs, "3.2 Ten strongest associations")
kable(top_pairs, caption = "Ten strongest associations between variables")
```

The strongest associations are among the travel variables themselves: main mode with seat availability (V = 0.58), distance with trip time (0.54), residence with main mode (0.53), access mode with egress mode (0.53), residence with travel budget (0.51) and trip time with departure time (0.50). Together they form a cluster of related travel characteristics: where students live determines their distance and mode, which in turn determine trip time, waiting time, transfers and cost. Apart from faculty and year of study (V = 0.38), the demographic and wellbeing variables are only weakly associated with the travel variables.

## 3.3 Which variables are most associated with stress level?

```{r stress-ranking, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 7}
rank_df <- data.frame(var = setdiff(cat_vars, "stress_level"))
rank_df$V <- cv_mat[rank_df$var, "stress_level"]
rank_df$p <- cv_p[rank_df$var, "stress_level"]
rank_df$Significance <- factor(ifelse(rank_df$p < 0.05, "Significant (p < 0.05)", "Not significant"),
                               levels = c("Significant (p < 0.05)", "Not significant"))
rank_df$Variable <- factor(short[rank_df$var], levels = short[rank_df$var][order(rank_df$V)])

p_rank <- ggplot(rank_df, aes(x = V, y = Variable, fill = Significance)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.2f", V)), hjust = -0.2, family = FONT, size = 3.8) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Significant (p < 0.05)" = "#2a78d6", "Not significant" = "#c3c2b7"),
                    name = "Chi-square test", drop = FALSE) +
  scale_x_continuous(name = "Cramér's V with stress level (bias-corrected)",
                     limits = c(0, max(rank_df$V) * 1.2 + 0.02),
                     expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0))) +
  scale_y_discrete(name = NULL) +
  theme_report() +
  theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.major.x = element_line(colour = "#e1e0d9", linewidth = 0.3))
save_fig(p_rank, "3.3_association_with_stress_level", width = 9, height = 7)
p_rank

rank_tab <- rank_df[order(-rank_df$V), c("Variable", "V", "p")]
rank_tab$V <- round(rank_tab$V, 3); rank_tab$p <- signif(rank_tab$p, 3)
names(rank_tab) <- c("Variable", "Cramér's V with stress level", "p-value")
rownames(rank_tab) <- NULL
add_table(rank_tab, "3.3 Association with stress level")
kable(rank_tab)
```

Trip time has the strongest association with stress level (V = 0.36, moderate), followed by main mode (0.30), feeling unsafe (0.27), egress mode (0.27) and waiting time (0.25). Access mode, vehicle changes, general stress (C4), residence, seat availability, year of study, gender and distance also have weak but significant associations (V = 0.16–0.23, p < 0.05). Crowding, sleep quality, travel budget, weather impact, departure time, workload pressure, faculty, days per week and late arrivals are not significantly associated with stress level. Some ordinal variables (for example distance, crowding and travel budget) appear stronger in the Spearman analysis (Section 3.1), because Cramér's V ignores the order of the categories and uses only the three stress levels.

```{r save-tables}
write_xlsx(c(list(Index = table_index), table_list), "tables/analysis-tables.xlsx")
```

All tables are saved in **tables/analysis-tables.xlsx** (the *Index* sheet lists
them) and all graphs are in the **figures** folder.
